paper_title: Factorized Context Attention: From Emulated to Native Grid Probing

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Models read a book, an hour of video, or an image in one forward pass. As the context grows, this pass slows down, loses accuracy, and stops at the context window. Sparse attention is efficient, but keeps the other two limitations. Grid probing, a recent training-free method, recovers the accuracy and extends the reach by asking a frozen model the same question about short local and strided spans of the input, but every question repeats the whole computation, since each span is encoded again. Our insight is that grid probing is emulated attention, an attention pattern reproduced from outside the model through prompts, since each probe only restricts which part of the input the question can see. We introduce Factorized Context Attention (FCA), a training-free block-sparse attention that runs the same pattern natively, as the attention of the model itself. FCA encodes the input once into a KV cache, reads all spans as masked sequences in one batched forward, and uses a stair position schedule to keep every span inside the trained position range. Across long video understanding, long-context text inference and image grounding, FCA matches the accuracy and the reach of grid probing at a fraction of its cost. It gains about 10 points over the single pass on long video and 9 to 14 points on long novels, finds needles in videos of over a thousand frames and in texts four times the length of the window, and answers a later question about the same input in as little as a tenth of the time of grid probing. Native attention thus keeps what emulated attention gains without its cost, all with existing frozen language and vision-language models.

Native attention thus keeps what emulated attention gains without its cost, all with existing frozen language and vision-language models. 1. Introduction Models answer questions about book or long video by reading the whole input in single forward pass, which we call the monolithic read. As the input grows, the monolithic read slows down, since its attention cost is quadratic, loses accuracy well before it reaches the context window [9, 16, Equal contribution. Corresponding author. Principal investigator. Code: https://github.com/mohammad2012191/FCA Figure 1. Emulated against native attention. (a) Grid probing builds the grid outside the frozen model and calls the model once per span. (b) FCA passes the input once and selects the spans inside the model with masked attention. 24, 29], and stops at the window. Sparse attention [19, 41] and cached serving [21] make the read faster, but neither restores its accuracy or lets it read past the window. recent line of training-free methods, which we refer to as grid probing, reads the input differently [1012]. Grid probing places the blocks of the input on hypothetical KK grid, asks frozen model the same question about each row (a local span) and each column (a strided span), and pools the 2K answers into one answer that reflects the whole input. Because every span is short, each read stays within the range that the model handles well, which reduces the noise of long contexts and extends the reach beyond the window. Short spans also keep the key-value cache small and manageable while matching or exceeding the accuracy of the monolithic read. This comes, however, at significant cost in speed and computation, as every span is separate prompt that is encoded again for every question and is not reused. Our key observation is that grid probing is attention in disguise. Each probe only decides which span of the input the question may attend to, which is exactly what an attention mask does. We therefore call grid probing emulated attention, since it reproduces an attention pattern from outside the model, one prompt at time, and we call the same pattern run inside the attention layers of the model native attention. Figure 1 contrasts the two. Emulated attention 1 needs only the outputs of model, so it runs on closed models and holds single span in memory, whereas native attention encodes the input once and reuses that encoding for every span and every question. We introduce Factorized Context Attention (FCA, Fig. 2), training-free block-sparse attention pattern that runs grid probing as native attention. FCA encodes the input once and stores its keys and values. It then answers each request with 2K masked sequences in one batched forward, each attending to one local or strided span, at positions that keep every span contiguous inside the trained range. FCA thereby inherits the accuracy, the reach and the evidence map of grid probing, while being faster and cacheable. Across long video, long text and single images, FCA matches the accuracy of grid probing at fraction of its time, and it gains most over the monolithic read where the input strains the model, by about 10 points on long video and 9 to 14 points on long novels. FCA also finds needles in videos of over thousand frames and in texts four times the window, which the monolithic read cannot reach.

sections.title: The main contributions of this work are summarized as
sections.content: follows: We introduce the distinction between emulated attention, an attention pattern reproduced from outside model through prompts, and native attention, the same pattern run inside its attention layers, and we characterize when each is the better choice. We propose Factorized Context Attention, trainingfree block-sparse attention pattern that runs grid probing natively from single encoding of the input. We show that FCA reproduces the local probes of grid probing up to shift of positions, and that it keeps the s1.5 encoding cost of grid probing while paying it once instead of for every question. 2. Related Work model that reads long context in single pass is slow, loses accuracy as the context grows, and stops at its window. Prior work addresses this problem along three lines. The first makes the attention of the pass cheaper, the second avoids encoding the same context twice, and the third avoids reading the whole context at once. Cheaper attention. The first line reduces the cost of attention over long context, with methods of two categories, (i) trained patterns, which build sparse pattern into the model, and (ii) training-free methods, which change how frozen model reads. Grid probing emulates an attention pattern through prompts, and FCA runs the same pattern natively. Post hoc means the method applies to frozen model with no training. Black-box means the read needs only the models next-token scores. Encode once means one encoding serves every question on context. Past window means reading contexts longer than the models window. windows with global tokens, with random connections in BigBird [4, 47], and recent models route each query to subset of the context, MoBA and NSA to blocks through block-scoring gate [26, 46] and DeepSeek-V3.2 to tokens through learned indexer [23]. All of these patterns are part of the architecture. The model must be trained from scratch or fine-tuned with the pattern, so none of them can be applied post hoc to frozen model. They also keep single pass over the whole context, so they still stop at the context window. In the second category, sparse prefills approximate the monolithic read with fewer attention computations [18, 19, 41], so they keep its window limit and its accuracy loss. Streaming methods read past the window with sliding window and memory [39, 40], but they drop distant context or retrieve it heuristically. Position interpolation stretches the window with little or no fine-tuning [30], but it still needs one long monolithic read, whose attention cost grows with the square of the context. Efficient kernels are orthogonal to both categories, since they compute the same attention with less memory traffic [6, 7] or compile arbitrary block masks [8]. Encoding context once. The second line leaves attention as it is and removes repeated work. Serving systems avoid encoding shared context again for every question by caching its keys and values [21] and batching many queries over it [20]. Parallel encoding goes further. It encodes every context alone and lets one query attend to all of them at once [27, 31, 44]. No cached block has seen any other, and accuracy drops unless the cache is repaired, by recomputing tokens [17, 45], by an anchor block [1], by calibrating the attention [44], or by fine-tuning [27]. In all of these methods one query still attends to every cached block, so its attention span grows with the context and the quality of the answer depends on how well the cache is repaired. This line saves time on later questions, but each question is still one 2 read over the whole context. Reading in short spans. The third line, grid probing, addresses the accuracy loss and the window limit directly, because it never lets one query read the whole context. Grid probing places the input on KK grid, asks frozen model the same question about each row and each column, and combines the 2K answers. GridProbe applies it to the frames of video and selects frames for second pass [11], AnswerMap to the bands of an image, to map where an answer comes from [10], and Periscope to the chunks of long text, which it reads past the window [12]. All three run at the prompt level, as emulated attention in our terms, so they read any model through its next-token scores and hold the memory of one probe. Their limitation is cost. Every probe is separate forward pass over its own copy of its span, so the input is encoded twice for every question, no encoding is reused from one question to the next, and every later question costs as much as the first. The three lines are complementary, and fast factorized read needs one thing from each, the bounded local and strided spans of grid probing, the single encoding of cached serving, and block-sparse pattern that frozen model can run on standard kernels. Properties and trade-offs Every sequence of FCA is an ordinary sequence over KV cache with padding mask, so FCA runs on standard attention kernels [6]. Emulated and native attention compute the same probes and differ in how they pay for them (Tab. 2). Native attention gains two things from encoding the context once, in rows that do not depend on each other. First, the encoding is reused by every request, so its cost, which grows as s1.5 as in grid probing [12], is paid once. Second, new input becomes new rows of the grid, which are encoded at cost that does not depend on what is already stored. Native attention pays for these gains in two ways. It keeps the encoding of the whole context in memory, as the monolithic read does, where emulated attention holds one span, and it needs the attention layers of the model, where emulated attention needs only its outputs. Emulated attention therefore suits closed models, tight memory budgets and single questions over inputs too large to keep, and native attention suits open models, inputs near or beyond the window, and repeated questions about one input. Both kinds of attention share one property that the monolithic read lacks. Their rows and their span sequences do not depend on each other, so the work and, for native attention, the store can be divided among devices, unlike causal pass over the whole context. Theoretically, with enough devices, the limit that remains is the position range of the model, which bounds the context at 2/(4c) tokens. 4. Experiments 4.1. Setup We compare three reads of the same frozen model, with the same prompt and read-out, the monolithic read as the reference, grid probing as the emulated read, and FCA as the native read. The emulated read is Periscope for text [12], GridProbe for video [11], and the strips of AnswerMap for single images [10]. XAttention [41] and Token Sparse Attention [19], two training-free sparse prefills of the monolithic read, serve as further references. Text experiments use Qwen3-4B [42] and Llama3.1-8B [14] on InfiniteBench En.MC [48], 229 questions over novels with median length of 150k tokens, and on SCBench [22], with blocks of c=500 tokens. Video experiments use InternVL3.5-2B [36], Qwen3-VL-2B and 8B [2] on LongVideoBench [38] and the long split of Video-MME [13], with 144 uniformly sampled frames on 1212 grid, as in GridProbe. Image experiments follow AnswerMap with Qwen3-VL-4B on RefCOCOg [28] and TextVQA [34]. We report accuracy, the time to first token for the first question on context (cold) and for later ones (warm), and peak GPU memory, all on one A100 80GB with FlashAttention-2 [6]. Conclusion and Limitations We showed that grid probing is emulated attention, an attention pattern reproduced from outside the model through 8 prompts, and introduced FCA, which runs the same pattern natively from single encoding of the input. Across video, text and images, FCA keeps the accuracy, the reach and the evidence maps of grid probing and answers every later request in fraction of its time, with existing frozen models. FCA has three limitations. It needs the attention layers of an open model, it keeps the encoding of the whole input in memory, and its strided probes approximate their emulated counterparts, so emulated attention remains the better choice for closed models and tight memory budgets. Future work can train model with the pattern, run other prompting strategies natively, and emulate other training-free attention patterns through prompts. We compare three reads of the same frozen model, the monolithic read as the reference, grid probing as the emulated read and FCA as the native read, with the same prompt and answer read-out and no training. F.1. Open-ended questions and conversations An open-ended question has no answer options to score, so each probe scores relevance. After the question, every span sequence asks whether the text above contains the information needed to answer it, and the probe score is the log-odds of Yes against No [12], with Yes in the role of an option and No in the role of the abstain option of Eq. (3). The scores are pooled into the evidence map as in Eq. (4), and the select read-out reads the blocks with the highest cells again, in their original order, with the question, and generates the answer. The direct read-out does not apply, since there are no options to choose among. In conversation, every turn is new request over the same store. The request of turn carries the previous questions and answers followed by the new question, so it grows with every turn, while the store never changes and the context is never encoded again. Each turn runs its full request in all 2K sequences and then discards it. This suits conversations with short turns, such as those of SCBench (Sec. 4.4), where the history stays at few hundred tokens. With long turns, the request itself would grow beyond the range that the model reads well and would be processed 2K times per turn. Long turns can instead enter the store as new local spans, encoded once each, which Sec. F.2 tests. F. Many questions on one input F.2. Conversations with long turns This section completes Sec. 4.4. Each of 8 conversations has 16 turns. Every turn adds 32k tokens of the En.MC novels with one needle sentence at 16 random place, as in the needle test, and asks for the number of needle from turn chosen uniformly among the turns so far. Scope and choice of read Section 3.4 compares emulated and native attention, and three points complete that comparison. First, FCA applies to every model whose layers keep per-token key-value cache, which covers all the language and vision-language models of Sec. 4. Second, the three reads serve different inputs. The monolithic read with prefix cache suits an input that fits the window with room to spare, grid probing suits closed models and small memory, and FCA suits inputs near or beyond the window and several questions about one input. Third, each probe reads one span, so evidence that is split across two blocks with no span in common is brought together by the select read. How block is encoded and where it is placed matter more than any other choice. block encoded alone starts without the text before it, and encoding each block within its local span instead adds several points of direct accuracy on Qwen3-4B and far more on Llama-3.1-8B (Tab. 10b). Positions decide whether the store can be read past the window. Document positions keep the order of the blocks but place the late spans of long novels beyond the window, which costs Llama-3.1-8B about third of its direct accuracy, and costs Qwen3-4B, whose 262k window holds most novels, only few points (Tab. 10c). Placing every block at the start instead keeps every position small but loses the order of the blocks within span, and loses far more accuracy (Tabs. 10b and 24a). Stair positions are the only assignment that keeps the order of every span and stays below 2 sc. Table 24 ablates three further parts of FCA on En.MC, how request reads the store, the block size and the execution. The factorized read is what lets frozen model use store of separately encoded blocks. On store of blocks encoded alone at the block start, one query over every block, as parallel encoding [31] reads it, collapses to chance and answers the same letter for almost every question, while the 2K span sequences of FCA over the same store score well above chance, most on Qwen3-4B (Tab. 24a). Methods that let one query read many separately encoded blocks finetune the model for it [27] or recalibrate its attention [44]. Hundreds of blocks at the same positions give one query an attention pattern that the frozen model never saw in training, while each sequence of FCA reads one span as contiguous text at trained positions. The block size is not sensitive choice. Periscope loses several points on LongBench v2 when its blocks double from 500 to 1,000 tokens [12], while the select accuracy of FCA stays within about two points between blocks of 250 and 1,000 tokens on both models (Tab. 24b). The execution choices change only time. Running the sequences one at time changes about as many answers as the batch shape alone (Sec. C.1) and makes later request slower, and pageable host store changes no answer and adds fraction of second where the store leaves the GPU.
